\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Wage Floors and Employment Retention:\\
Evidence from a Regional Mandate}
\author{L.~Beaumont, C.~Okafor, and M.~Hale}
\date{March 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We study a regional wage-floor mandate that bound only firms
above a size threshold, and we estimate its effect on the
twelve-month employment retention of low-wage workers. Using
a difference-in-differences design that exploits the threshold,
we find that the mandate raised retention by 4.2 percentage
points without measurable effects on hiring or on hours.
Event-study estimates are flat before the reform, and the
effect is concentrated in establishments that reported binding
floors ex ante. We read the pattern as evidence of monopsonistic
competition in local labour markets.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Do wage floors destroy jobs? The canonical competitive model
says they must, yet a long empirical tradition has struggled
to find the predicted losses. This paper studies a setting in
which the mandate bound some firms and not others, so that
the counterfactual is observed rather than assumed.
Our setting is the Northern Province wage-floor reform of
2019. The reform applied to private establishments with fifty
or more employees and raised the minimum hourly wage for the
bottom decile by roughly a fifth. Establishments below the
threshold were explicitly exempt, and enforcement records show
that compliance among covered firms was near universal.
We link the establishment register to quarterly payroll
filings and follow every low-wage worker for three years.
The linked panel lets us measure retention, hiring, hours,
and earnings at the worker level, and the size threshold
supplies a comparison group whose trends we verify directly.
Three findings emerge. First, retention among low-wage
workers rose sharply in covered establishments relative to
exempt ones. Second, we detect no offsetting margin: hiring
held steady, hours moved little, and separations fell rather
than rose. Third, the effect is largest precisely where
pre-reform wage dispersion suggests monopsony power.
The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2
describes the reform and its enforcement. Section 3 presents
the data. Section 4 lays out the empirical strategy, Section 5
reports the estimates, and Section 6 discusses interpretation.

\section{Institutional Background}
The reform was announced in March 2019 and took effect the
following January. Coverage was defined by establishment size
in the reference quarter, so firms could not shrink below the
threshold to avoid the mandate once the baseline was fixed.
Enforcement combined automatic payroll audits with a worker
hotline. Administrative penalties were rare in practice,
because the audit trail made underpayment easy to detect and
costly to defend. Surveys fielded by the statistical office
indicate that covered establishments raised base pay for the
affected decile within two quarters of the effective date.

\section{Data}
Our analysis file links three administrative sources. The
establishment register provides size, sector, and location.
Quarterly payroll filings provide earnings, hours, and tenure
for every employee. The reform roster records coverage status
and the audit history of each establishment.
We restrict the sample to private establishments that filed
in every quarter from 2017 to 2021, and we define low-wage
workers as those in the bottom decile of the pre-reform
establishment wage distribution. The final panel covers
41{,}206 worker-quarter observations in the balanced sample,
of which 40{,}884 remain after the control variables are
merged. Summary statistics appear in the online appendix.

\section{Empirical Strategy}
We estimate the event-study specification
\begin{equation}
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t
+ \sum_{k \neq -1} \beta_k \, D_i \times \mathbf{1}[t - t_0 = k]
+ X_{it}'\gamma + u_{it},
\end{equation}
where $D_i$ marks covered establishments and the coefficients
$\beta_k$ trace the dynamic effect relative to the quarter
before the reform. Our preferred specification aggregates the
post-reform coefficients into a single estimate
\begin{equation}
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta_1 \, D_i \times Post_t
+ X_{it}'\gamma + u_{it},
\end{equation}
with standard errors clustered by establishment. The
identifying assumption is that exempt establishments trace
the counterfactual path of covered ones, an assumption we
probe with pre-trend tests and with placebo thresholds.

\section{Results}
Table \ref{tab:main} reports the headline estimates. Column
(1) includes no controls, column (2) adds firm controls, and
column (3) adds worker controls; the point estimate is stable
across the three columns, which reassures us that selection
on observables is limited.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Effect of the mandate on twelve-month retention}
\label{tab:main}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & (1) & (2) & (3) \\
\midrule
Treated $\times$ Post & 0.38 & 0.40 & 0.42 \\
 & (0.09) & (0.10) & (0.11) \\
Firm controls & No & Yes & Yes \\
Worker controls & No & No & Yes \\
\midrule
Observations & 41{,}206 & 41{,}206 & 40{,}884 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Hiring rates, average hours, and separation hazards are
reported in the appendix; none of these margins moves enough
to account for the retention gain. Placebo thresholds at
forty and sixty employees produce estimates near zero, and
the pre-reform event-study coefficients are jointly
insignificant in every specification we have tried.

\section{Discussion}
The magnitude of the estimate deserves emphasis. Because the
reform bound only firms above the size threshold, the coefficient
$\beta_1 = 0.42$ (s.e.\ 0.11) in column (3) of Table \ref{tab:main}
is interpretable as the causal effect of the mandate on the
probability that a low-wage worker retains employment for at
least twelve months. The implied payroll increase of 7\% is
an order of magnitude smaller than a competitive spot-market
model would predict, and the gap---already visible in the raw
event-study traces---points toward monopsonistic wage setting
rather than toward efficient bargaining. For the average
treated establishment with 1{,}980 worker-months at risk, the
estimate translates into roughly eighty additional worker-years.

A competing account emphasises labour--labour substitution:
perhaps covered establishments retained low-wage workers
only because they dismissed their close substitutes. The
occupation-level estimates do not support this account, since
retention rose within every occupation cell we can form,
including the cells with the closest available substitutes.
A second competing account credits the simultaneous training
subsidy. The subsidy, however, was available to covered and
exempt establishments on identical terms, so it cannot explain
the differential retention we estimate at the threshold.
We caution that the estimate is local to the bottom decile
and to a mandate of moderate size. Larger floors, or floors
that bind higher in the wage distribution, could well have
different effects, and our design is silent about both.

\section{Conclusion}
A size-contingent wage floor raised the twelve-month retention
of low-wage workers by about four percentage points, with no
measurable offset on hiring, hours, or separations. The
pattern fits a monopsonistic labour market better than a
competitive one, and it suggests that moderate wage floors
can redistribute earnings toward low-wage workers without
destroying their jobs. We leave the analysis of larger
mandates, and of floors that bind higher in the distribution,
to future work as further reforms unfold.
\end{document}
